sources.title: Williamina Fleming (Q284180), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-18): English label 'Williamina Fleming' (no native English description; the API returns the Spanish fallback 'astronoma escocesa (1857-1911)'), Korean label 윌리어미나 플레밍, instance of human, born 1857-05-15, died 1911-05-21, citizenship United States and United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, occupation astronomer. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Elizabeth D. Schafer, 'Fleming, Williamina Paton (1857-1911)', Women in World History: A Biographical Encyclopedia (Gale, reproduced on Encyclopedia.com; read in full including its source list). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: her work on the Harvard College Observatory's photographs of stellar spectra for the Henry Draper Memorial under Edward C. Pickering, the 1890 Draper Catalogue of Stellar Spectra (more than 10,000 stars described in the 'Pickering-Fleming System'), more than 300 variable stars, ten novae and gaseous nebulae found on the plates, her 1898 appointment as curator of astronomical photographs (the first woman given an official appointment by Harvard's governing board), and her supervision of a staff of mostly women who examined and catalogued almost 200,000 plates. The entry quotes Pickering, Annie Jump Cannon, E. Dorrit Hoffleit, Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin and Owen Gingerich, and draws on her own 1900 diary, where she complained that administration left too little time for research and that her pay was below the men's. It notes that the plates' poor quality forced extra classes and that she had trouble keeping her classes in a consistent order; that Pickering read her 1898 paper to the audience because she had not credited herself; and that Payne-Gaposchkin recalled her as a strict 'martinet' who was not beloved. It says she 'discovered' white dwarf stars in 1910, a claim other sources word differently and which is not repeated. Modern biographical encyclopedia entry, admiring but candid about limits and costs.

Annie J. Cannon, 'Williamina Paton Fleming', Science vol. 33, no. 861, 30 June 1911, pp. 987-988 (Internet Archive scan of the JSTOR Early Journal Content, read in full). Contemporary obituary by a Harvard colleague: Fleming's duties were to examine, index and care for the photographic plates; she examined all spectrum plates from Cambridge and Arequipa with a magnifying glass and marked every object with peculiar spectra, finding ten new stars and more than 300 variable stars from the bright lines in their spectra; she classified the spectra of 10,351 stars published in 1890 in the Draper Catalogue; much of her time was taken by proofreading the Annals; and 'her diligence and patience were combined with great self-reliance and courage.' Also lists her honours (honorary member of the Royal Astronomical Society in 1906, a gold medal of the Astronomical Society of Mexico). Colleague's obituary, written within a month of her death, so admiring and a Harvard insider's view.

Joseph L. Spradley, 'Williamina Paton Stevens Fleming', EBSCO Research Starters: History (2024; read in full): in 1886 she was put in charge of the Draper project to measure, analyse and classify stellar spectra; in the 1890 Draper Catalogue she measured 28,266 spectra on 633 plates taken with the eight-inch Bache telescope and classified 10,351 stars brighter than seventh magnitude; Pickering acknowledged that she did most of the work; she found that stars with bright emission lines were variable, which gave a tool for finding long-period variables, and she described 222 variable stars in her 1907 study; she discovered ten novae and many Wolf-Rayet stars; Annie Jump Cannon later reorganised her letter classes into the Harvard sequence, and Henrietta Leavitt began as her assistant. The numbers of classes and of nebulae differ among sources (Spradley says fifteen categories, Schafer seventeen). Short reference article, admiring.

Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, 'Following Her Stars' education site, pages 'Williamina P. Fleming' and 'Nebulae' (both read): calls her the first curator of the Astronomical Photographic Glass Plate Collection who led and mentored the Women Astronomical Computers, says she documented more than 10,000 stars, 310 variable stars, 10 novae and 52 nebulae including the Horsehead Nebula, managed the Henry Draper Memorial and organised the publication of the Annals, spoke at the 1893 Chicago World's Fair congress, and was the first American woman elected an honorary member of the Royal Astronomical Society (1906). Two pages of the sister site on her variable-star and administrative work returned an access-denied page (a bot wall) and were not read. Observatory-owned educational site, self-interested and admiring.

Dava Sobel, 'Williamina Fleming', Scientist of the Day, Linda Hall Library, 15 May 2020 (read in full; by the author of The Glass Universe, a history of the Harvard women): says the popular story of Pickering's exclaiming 'my maid could do a better job' is apocryphal; that she found more than 200 variable stars and about fifty nebulae and picked out the Horsehead Nebula's shape on an 1888 plate; that she divided stars into more than a dozen spectral types with a letter each, which Cannon later conflated into OBAFGKM; that her work ethic was legendary; that Pickering promoted her in 1899 to a post he created for her, the first Harvard University title held by a woman, with a team of eleven or more women; and that her handwritten contribution to Harvard's Chest of 1900 time capsule said Pickering kept her salary of $1,500 below men's in comparable positions. Independent popular-history writer, admiring, correcting legend.

Natasha Geiling, 'The Women Who Mapped the Universe and Still Couldn't Get Any Respect', Smithsonian Magazine, 18 September 2013 (read in full): describes the Harvard computers, who numbered more than 80 under Pickering, worked six-day weeks for 25 to 50 cents an hour (about half a man's pay) on mostly clerical duties, and were nicknamed 'Pickering's Harem'; the section on Fleming quotes her diary describing 12 women engaged in the care of the photographs and says Pickering replaced a male assistant with her, which Sobel calls apocryphal. Used only for the working conditions around her; Fleming is a minor subject of the article. Popular magazine feature, critical of Pickering's limits.

detail_orientation.rationale: [src_fleming_cannon, src_fleming_schafer, src_fleming_spradley, src_fleming_cfa | 1881-1911 | colleague's obituary, encyclopedia entry, reference article, observatory site] Cannon says she examined all spectrum plates from Cambridge and Peru with a magnifying glass and marked every object with a peculiar spectrum, indexed each fragile plate and did the tedious proofreading of the Annals; Schafer says she monitored every plate and checked her assistants' work; Spradley counts 28,266 spectra measured on 633 plates. The accounts describe method and workload, not individual slips or corrections. CONCENTRATION (agent): lowered from 78 / 0.64 because the modern accounts rest on Cannon's and Pickering's own descriptions, so there is really one Harvard-insider family plus one modern retelling.

discipline.rationale: [src_fleming_schafer, src_fleming_sobel, src_fleming_smithsonian | 1890s-1911 | encyclopedia entry, history column, magazine feature] Schafer, drawing on her diary, says she rarely took vacations and worked late into the night for Pickering, and quotes Hoffleit and Payne-Gaposchkin on her reputation as a strict disciplinarian; Sobel calls her work ethic legendary; the magazine feature notes six-day weeks for the computers generally. The long hours are largely her own account and the workplace norm, and Payne-Gaposchkin adds she was not beloved, so impact is dual-edged. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 72 / 0.55 and the evidence type from strong inference to inference because the long hours come from her own diary and from reputation rather than a documented pattern of routines.

persistence.rationale: [src_fleming_cannon, src_fleming_schafer | 1881-1911 | colleague's obituary, encyclopedia entry] She stayed in the plate work for thirty years until her death; Cannon says she was at work on a memoir on peculiar spectra when she fell ill, and Schafer says she attended a solar-research meeting in 1910 despite serious illness and wrote her final paper while ill. The illness details come from one entry. CONCENTRATION (agent): lowered from 70 / 0.55 because the late-illness episodes come from a single modern entry and tenure alone is a weak sign of persistence.

analytical_rigor.rationale: [src_fleming_spradley, src_fleming_schafer, src_fleming_cannon, src_fleming_sobel | 1886-1907 | reference article, encyclopedia entry, colleague's obituary, history column] She built a classification from photographed spectra where, Cannon says, no precedents existed, found that red stars with bright emission lines are variable and used that as a tool to find more of them (Spradley), and described 222 variables with comparison sequences; but Schafer says poor plates created extra classes and she struggled to order her classes consistently, and Cannon later reorganised the scheme. Impact is dual-edged. CONCENTRATION (agent): lowered from 70 / 0.55 because the claims for her method rest on two reference summaries of one Harvard record.

systems_abstraction.rationale: [src_fleming_schafer, src_fleming_sobel, src_fleming_spradley | 1886-1890 | encyclopedia entry, history column, reference article] She was given responsibility for a letter-coded classification of stellar spectra, published in the 1890 Draper Catalogue as the Pickering-Fleming system, which Cannon later reordered into the sequence still used. The scheme was a joint project with Pickering, and no source describes how she reasoned about it. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 62 / 0.5 and the evidence type from strong inference to inference because credit for the system is shared with Pickering and was largely replaced by Cannon's version.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_fleming_schafer, src_fleming_sobel | 1890-1900 | encyclopedia entry, history column] Schafer says she claimed work in her own name rather than Pickering's when she could, spoke at the 1893 Chicago congress urging observatory directors to hire women, and hired assistants including Cannon and Maury; Sobel says she wrote her pay grievance into the Chest of 1900 time capsule. Pickering's promotion of her was a large part of her advancement, and the evidence comes from two modern summaries. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 66 / 0.5 and the evidence type from strong inference to inference because all the episodes come from the same two modern accounts.

leadership_drive.rationale: [src_fleming_schafer, src_fleming_sobel, src_fleming_cfa, src_fleming_spradley | 1898-1911 | encyclopedia entry, history column, observatory site, reference article] In 1898 she became curator of astronomical photographs, the first woman appointed by Harvard's governing board, and supervised a staff of eleven or more women (dozens by some accounts) who examined and catalogued nearly 200,000 plates; she recruited and interviewed workers; Hoffleit remembered the awe in which she was held, and Payne-Gaposchkin called her a martinet who was not beloved, so impact is dual-edged. The sources describe offices and recollections, not specific management decisions. CONCENTRATION (agent): lowered from 68 / 0.55 because the observatory site, the encyclopedia and the reference article repeat the same appointment and team-size facts.

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: STRONG (Stage B) / lead SURVIVED with caveats: the lead is the plate printed with a captioned portrait in Technical World Magazine vol. 6 no. 2 (October 1906). Holder facts checked: the HathiTrust catalogue API record for Harvard's copy hvd.32044048683122 (volume 'v.6 (1906-07)', original holder Harvard University) gives rights code 'pd' and 'Full view'; the HathiTrust page itself is behind a Cloudflare challenge and was not opened (recorded as a bot wall, not a rights conflict), so the printed caption was read from the Commons file description, which transcribes it as 'Mrs. Williamina Paton Fleming. World's champion star-discoverer, signally honored by the Royal Astronomical Society of England'; the image extract is cropped to the portrait and carries no lettering, and no Internet Archive copy of volume 6 exists to cross-check. Commons says photographer not named, date 'no later than October 1906', PD-US-expired. The sitter is also consistent with the same woman in Harvard Observatory photographs (not compared in detail). KIND likeness (a halftone of a photograph of her, published during her life). The Wikimedia upload server rate-limited downloads for a while (HTTP 429, retry-after 600 s); the file was then fetched through the thumbnail route Wikimedia recommends (500 px wide, downscaled from the 590 x 660 original, converted to JPEG); no limit was bypassed. The alternative (Commons 'circa 1890s' Harvard Observatory image, 1463 x 1894) was not used: its Commons rationale is US-only and warns about non-US status, the author is unknown and there is no documented publication chain. PREFLIGHT: QID VERIFIED LIVE (2026-11-18, Wikidata API) Q284180 label 'Williamina Fleming', no native English description (Spanish fallback 'astronoma escocesa (1857-1911)'), ko label 윌리어미나 플레밍, instance of human, born 1857-05-15, died 1911-05-21, citizenship US and UK, occupation astronomer. REGION north_america as assigned (precedent Alexander Graham Bell and John Muir for Scottish-born Americans), ERA 19th_century, nationality GB and US. KOREAN NAME 윌리어미나 플레밍 is the Wikidata label; the Korean Wikipedia-style transliteration is used, and no separate traditional name exists. PRIVATE LIFE: sources describe her marriage, her husband's departure, her pregnancy and her first job as a household maid; this is private-life context, it is not used as evidence for any row and no inference is drawn. Her suffrage activity is political context, also not scored. ATTRIBUTION: attributable (dated catalogue, obituary, publications; the contemporary obituary by Cannon and Pickering-era records). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Elizabeth D. Schafer, Women in World History entry (src_fleming_schafer). READ (6 sources besides Wikidata): Schafer entry (full); Cannon's 1911 Science obituary (full); Spradley EBSCO article (full); Harvard-Smithsonian CfA 'Following Her Stars' pages (Fleming and Nebulae; the two Plate Stacks pages were access-denied); Sobel's Linda Hall column (full); Geiling Smithsonian Magazine feature (full). Wikipedia not used. Also read but not cited: the Physics Today note (derivative), a Scottish-history blog reprint that says the credit for the Horsehead Nebula went to Pickering (an uncorroborated blog claim, so the cards only say 'Harvard and Sobel credit her'), the National Library of Scotland page (empty). NOT OPENED: Pickering's 1911 memorial, Bailey 1931, Jones and Boyd 1971, Sobel's book, Fleming's own 1893 paper and 1900 diary (known only through Schafer and Sobel), the Technical World article text. PERSPECTIVES: (1) colleague's obituary (Cannon), (2) modern biographical encyclopedia (Schafer) and reference article (Spradley), (3) observatory education site (CfA), (4) popular-history writer (Sobel), (5) magazine feature on the computers (Geiling). COUNTER-VOICES: Schafer on classification defects, on credit going first to Pickering and on staff memories (Payne-Gaposchkin: not beloved); Geiling and Sobel on pay and clerical limits; Sobel on the apocryphal maid story. CONTRADICTIONS AND LIMITS: counts differ among sources (nebulae 52 or 59; variables 200+, 222 or 300+; classes fifteen or seventeen or 'more than a dozen'); curatorship 1898 (Schafer, Spradley) or 1899 (Sobel, Physics Today); the white dwarf credit is worded differently by Schafer, Sobel and Physics Today so is left out of the cards; the maid-to-computer story is partly legend (Sobel). No adversarial biography exists; the independent critical angle is on pay and credit. Sparse 7-row profile by design (no rows for creativity, curiosity or risk: the sources document method and administration, not motives). SELF-CALIBRATION: reviewed all 9 initial rows; removed adaptability (job changes were assigned by Pickering) and collaboration (partnership and team supervision are already covered by the leadership row); lowered the remaining 7, see handback. MAJOR ACHIEVEMENT GATE: PASS on all (spectral classification; variable stars, novae and nebulae; curatorship and team). HANDBACK68 in TGI-r68-scratch/handback/williamina-fleming.json.

portrait.source: Halftone photograph of Williamina Paton Fleming printed with the caption 'Mrs. Williamina Paton Fleming. World's champion star-discoverer, signally honored by the Royal Astronomical Society of England.' in Technical World Magazine, volume 6, number 2 (October 1906, Chicago: Technical World Company); Harvard University's copy digitised in HathiTrust (hvd.32044048683122, volume 6, 1906-07; the HathiTrust catalogue record gives rights code 'pd', full view). The file is the 500-pixel-wide Wikimedia Commons thumbnail of the extract of the printed plate (original 590 x 660), converted to JPEG: a downscale only, no upscaling. The original-size download was rate-limited by Wikimedia (HTTP 429) so the sanctioned thumbnail route was used. The photographer is not named and the underlying photograph's original date is not documented.
portrait.license: Public domain: published in the United States in 1906 (before 1931); the HathiTrust record for the Harvard copy marks the volume public domain with full view. The photographer is unnamed, so there is no creator-death basis, but the publication date alone suffices
